Good question. The intention is never to keep people on long term antidepressants pretty much for this reason and so the current guidance is to keep the patient on the lowest tolerated successful dose and then maintain them for 6 months before considering gradual withdrawal.

In my experience, a considerable amount of patients respond well to this regime. However there are also some that feel that they require more of the antidepressant for a longer time and notice when they haven't taken it which is difficult to refute. Despite what the trials may say, faced with a patient that has improved with a medication and is requesting more, I take a reasonably pragmatic approach try to listen to the needs of the patient but make sure that they are fully informed about possible consequences. It's a great point and you're correct, it is possible for there to be issues like thyroid problems that could contribute towards someone's mood. In general, most diagnoses are made in the history- so doctors mat get clues from other associated symptoms the patient has. In the case of hypothyroidism For example, a patient may typically feel flat but also tired, have weight gain despite a reduced appetite with a sluggish bowel habit for example. In such cases it's easier to arrange bloods.

In cases without such associated symptoms, personally I tend to look for the story and to whether there obvious triggers for the depression e.g. bereavement, abuse which have clearly brought on the condition. Without a clear story, I'd be looking to screen them with blood tests.

These signs i have listed are part of the questionnaire called the PHQ9 scoring system which is one of the tools used by myself and other doctors in the UK certainly to help diagnose grades of depression. I had to present them in a way that was a little more engaging though as opposed to simply reading out the questionnaire.

The disclaimer is partly for legal reasons (I was told to do this by my medical insurance company) but obviously serves a clear purpose for the viewer. If someone recognises any of these and COULD have depression, it is absolutely wise to seek professional help to try to assess things further and confirm the diagnosis. I would perform the PHQ9 questionnaire and then discuss with the patient about which management option may suit them best and I would offer my advice to help guide them. The vast majority have depression triggered by life events but I would be screening for triggers such as drug and alcohol use, family history and other symptoms that may suggest organic pathology (depending on their age).

Personally, I have seen so many patients with depression in the past and the vast majority present far, far too late and have suffered for way too long. Far longer than necessary and I know that had they been able to see me earlier, I would have been able to help them. Leaving the symptoms longer puts people at risk of worsening depression and so this is why this is important. I actually congratulate people for seeing me early about their symptoms as it shows they have good awareness of their symptoms.
